fullText:
Palm Beach County — home to President Donald Trump’s Mar-a-Lago — passed a one-year moratoriam on the planning and construction of data centers as commissioners seek to conduct a thorough review of data centers’ impacts on the environment, noise pollution, and electric bills.

The moratorium, passed on Thursday, comes just weeks after Trump said that communities that reject data centers would "end up being backwards and poor." Among the wealthiest counties in the country, Palm Beach County includes the town of Palm Beach, home to 65 billionaires.

"If you want to go through poverty, crime and squalor, I would say don’t approve of data centers," Trump said from the Oval Office on Sep. 4.

The Palm Beach County Commissioners’ 6-0 vote doesn’t put a permanent ban on data centers. Instead, it gives county leadership time to conduct environmental impact reviews before updating zoning rules for where data centers can be built.

TRUMP’S DATA CENTER PUSH FRACTURES CONGRESS AS LOCAL ANGER EXPLODES: 'GRASPING AT STRAWS'

The moratorium applies to all new applications for data centers with an anticipated peak electrical load of at least 50 megawatts.

"Many communities want the economic benefits a data center brings, but we all fear the higher power bills, the negative environmental impact, disruptive noise, the depletion of water resources," a Palm Beach County resident shared during Thursday’s meeting.

Trump has made expanding data centers and accelerating artificial intelligence a cornerstone of his agenda, arguing that the United States cannot afford to lose the AI race to China and warning that opposition to data centers only benefits Beijing.

Data centers are the physical backbone of artificial intelligence, housing thousands of powerful computers that store and process digital information while providing the computing power needed to train and run AI systems.

Palm Beach County has already approved in 2016 the construction of "Project Tango" — a proposed 202-acre AI data center, which is located 20 miles from Mar-a-Lago. The data center will also be built near an elementary school and homes.

FOX NEWS POLL: VOTERS QUESTION WHETHER AI’S PROMISE OUTWEIGHS ITS RISKS

In July, commissioners voted 6-1 to reject a proposal to expand Project Tango by roughly 1.67 million square feet. But existing approvals for two 100,000-square-foot data center buildings remain in place.

Residents at the Thursday meeting said Project Tango was the driving factor behind the push to hit pause on data center project approvals, with several residents advocating for no data centers to be built.

"I think the best good neighbor data center is no data center," resident Sergei Kelly said. "We have the Everglades to our South and to our West. The coast to our East. I don’t think data centers, especially large data centers they want to build desperately should be here at all."

Fox News Digital reached to the White House and Palm Beach County Commissioners for comment.

title: Trump says U.S.-Iran talks will continue this week despite rejecting latest offer
description:
U.S. and Iranian officials said Sunday they still see a chance of a negotiated solution to the Iran war despite President Donald Trump's rejection of Tehran's latest offer.
Trump told Axios on Sunday that he expected U.S.
fullText:
U.S. and Iranian officials said Sunday they still see a chance of a negotiated solution to the Iran war despite President Donald Trump's rejection of Tehran's latest offer.

Trump told Axios on Sunday that he expected U.S. negotiators to continue indirect talks with Iran this week.

But hostile rhetoric on both sides underscored the difficulty of any diplomatic efforts.

"We are fully prepared for the war to be resumed. … We stand firm in the face of any new aggression, even if it comes to a doomsday war," Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told NBC News on Sunday. At the same time, he said, "we stand ready for diplomacy. It is up to President Trump to choose."

"If they are serious that they want a deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, now there is the possibility," Araghchi said.

On Saturday, Trump said he had rejected Iran's latest proposal to end the war. "They want to make a deal where they open the strait immediately because they're losing so badly," Trump told reporters.

But Axios reported that Trump had confirmed during a Sunday phone interview that there were plans for indirect talks.

"I expect more talks with Iran [this week]. They want to make a deal, but it is not the deal that I want to make. It is what we would have maybe agreed to a year ago. They overplayed their hand," Trump said, according to Axios.

U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz told NBC News's "Meet the Press" that the recent Iranian proposal was a "cynical attempt to put something on the table that they knew was unacceptable." The proposal included demands that the United States lift sanctions on Iran, release frozen assets and end the U.S. naval blockade on Iranian ports, he said.

"At the end of the day, of course, this has to end in some type of arrangement. But he's going to leave all options on the table to get there," Waltz told NBC News.

Araghchi had said Tehran's offer was similar to the memorandum of understanding both sides reached in June.

Both Araghchi and Waltz accused the other's country of engaging in negotiations only to violate their terms.

"Again they offered negotiation, again we accepted, and again they attacked us in the middle of negotiations. … But I am still trying diplomacy because I think we shouldn't miss any chance for peace," Araghchi said.

Waltz told NBC News it was "common sense" that the president did not have much confidence in Iran's offer after the country violated the memorandum of understanding brokered in June.

Negotiations between Iran and the U.S., both directly and indirectly, to end the war have been on and off since a few weeks after it began on Feb. 28.

In June, both countries reached an initial truce, signing a memorandum of understanding that included a two-month timeline to hammer out terms for lasting peace, including tackling differences over Iran's nuclear program, sanctions and control over the Strait of Hormuz.

The ceasefire quickly unraveled, and the 60-day deadline passed last month with no breakthroughs. Iranian officials pursued a flurry of diplomatic meetings in New York last week during the U.N. General Assembly. Trump administration officials held talks with the Iranian delegation through mediators, U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff said in an X post.

Trump had told the U.N. General Assembly on Tuesday that Iran could make a deal to end the war or face "annihilation." The Iranian delegation walked out of the chamber.

The following day, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian told the U.N. that Iran was "ready for dialogue and diplomacy and negotiations without accepting the language of force."

title: Bellamy 'hurting' as Denmark outclass Wales
description: Craig Bellamy says he is "hurting" on the back of Wales' 2-0 Nations League A defeat away to Denmark, but feels his side will continue to improve.
fullText:
Craig Bellamy says he is "hurting" after admitting Denmark were worthy winners against his Wales side in Copenhagen.

A Ben Davies own goal along with Gustav Isaksen's strike earned Brian Riemer's men a 2-0 victory over Wales at Parken Stadium.

It leaves Bellamy's team winless in six matches in 2026 and without a point from their away Nations League A double-header with Portugal and the Danes.

Despite the loss, Bellamy remains confident his side will improve by playing against Europe's elite on a consistent basis.

"I'm really hurting. When you see an athletic team run over you a little bit... but then, will we improve? I think we will," said the Wales head coach.

"This team will get better, these players will keep improving. There are young ones coming in well after I'm gone.

"For me now it's just focus, two more games to go. How can I help you improve for the next two games but also how can I improve?

"I'm probably more loving when I'm losing, I'm probably more of a pain in the backside when I'm winning."

Denmark dominated early on and Mikkel Damsgaard fired against the post shortly after Isaksen had a goal disallowed for offside.

Despite an improvement from Wales after the opening half an hour, they were ultimately undone from two set-pieces.

"I said to the players before the game, 'this is going to be tougher than Portugal'," Bellamy added.

"It was a different challenge but a very difficult one. The best team won overall.

"As disappointed as I am with that, the result I probably think was fair."

Nations League: Wales well beaten by Denmark - reaction

'Workhorse' Koumas growing with Wales

Defeat - which came just three days after a 1-0 loss to Portugal in Lisbon - has left Wales with plenty of work to do.

They will at least have home advantage at Cardiff City Stadium as they prepare for the remainder of the current international break, with matches against Norway on Thursday, 1 October, and then Denmark the following Sunday.

Captain Davies felt Wales were being taught some harsh lessons in what is their second stint in the top tier of the Nations League.

"It was a tough game. They are a good team and made it a hard game for us," the Spurs defender told BBC Match of the Day Wales.

"It was really frustrating to concede from two set-pieces. The Nations League games are against the best teams in Europe, it was always going to be tough.

"If you're not at 100% then you are going to get punished at this level. We have to regroup and go again on Thursday."

Despite the setback in the Danish capital, winger Sorba Thomas echoed Bellamy's sentiments.

"Thankfully we've got two games at home still to come. We'll have home advantage so we need to show a reaction," he told BBC Match of the Day Wales.

"We are just going to get better. We are a small nation but we've got big hearts and beliefs and for us it's about showing that more on the pitch."

title: Heroic York rearguard stuns Wigan in Grand Final
description: York Valkyrie become the first side to win the Women's Super League three times after an incredible defensive effort thwarts favourites Wigan.
fullText:
Betfred Women's Super League Grand Final

York Valkyrie became the first side to win the Women's Super League three times after an incredible defensive effort thwarted Wigan Warriors at the Brick Community Stadium.

Under siege for much of a scoreless second half, York stood firm to claim a surprise win over the favourites.

Teenager Amelie Lenham, the player of the match, led the way with a series of crucial interventions as a first-half try from Sinead Peach, plus two goals from Ellie Williamson, proved just enough.

Wigan - who had their only try-scorer Mia-Jayne Atherton and Eva Hunter sin-binned in the first half - were left stunned after an uncharacteristically error-strewn display.

York head coach Leon Pryce felt Hunter should have been sent off for a forearm to the throat of Williamson as she carried the ball into contact but in the end it did not affect the result.

The Valkyrie, the only team to have beaten Wigan this season, dug deep into their well of resolve to shade a gripping Grand Final.

Without the influential Tara Jane Stanley through concussion, they were odds against but with Wigan unable to get into their free-flowing stride, York's superb determination saw them over the line.

They had a simple gameplan and played it to perfection.

Peach gave them a ninth-minute lead, spinning through the Wigan defence close to the line after making the initial break as they dominated the opening exchanges.

Atherton pulled Wigan level in the 18th minute after a fine break from Jenna Foubister. But she was then sin-binned for her part in a dangerous double tip tackle with Bethan Dainton on Jas Bell, and Williamson put over the penalty to restore York's lead.

Lenham went close to increasing it and Liv Wood was held up over the line just after the break but from then it was one-way traffic.

But York, winners in 2023 and 2024, simply refused to yield.

Lisa Parker, who played with a broken hand, made 47 tackles. Her fiance proposed to her on the touchline afterwards. She said yes. It was that sort of night.

York Valkyrie's Agnes Wood told BBC Radio York:

"That was incredible. All the girls worked so hard. It was massive from everyone.

"In the second half Wigan really gave it back and the biggest thing we had to do was scramble and make sure that they didn't score. That was the main aim of the second half.

"We were all really motivated by the fact that nobody was giving us any credit and we really wanted to prove everyone wrong. We didn't have the strongest start to the season, but have we proved everyone wrong?

"All the coaching staff have backed us 100% from beginning to end and they just said to keep going and keep going and we have and I'm just so proud of all the girls. They've put in so much work throughout the whole season."

Wigan: Banks; Davies, Wilson, M Jones, Derbyshire; Foubister, Rowe; Coleman, Wilton, Sams, E. Hunter, C Jones, Williams

Interchanges: Marsh, Atherton, Dainton, Salihi

York: Donovan; Kershaw, Woods, Leniham, Partington; Akwiwu, Williamson; A. Wood, Peach, Pakulis, O. Wood, Andrade, Parker

Interchanges: Bell, Bibby, Brennan, Henderson

title: England win series as Banton delivers on potential
description: Tom Banton delivers on all of his potential by crashing a brilliant first international century as England wrapped up their summer with an ODI series win over Sri Lanka.
fullText:
Third Metro Bank one-day international, Kia Oval

England 355-7 (50 overs): Banton 126, Brook 77, Cox 76

Sri Lanka 132 (29.1 overs): Kusal 35; Dawson 3-26

Tom Banton delivered on all of his potential by crashing a brilliant first international century as England wrapped up their summer with an ODI series win over Sri Lanka.

The 27-year-old right-hander was once the rising star of English cricket when handed a debut in 2019 but afterwards fell out of love with the game after losing his way.

After reaching his hundred in 95 balls in the third one-day international at The Oval, he stood with arms wide and looked to the sky - all of that disappointment seemingly behind him.

"My fiance, Lilly, was here and all of her family," Banton said.

"Unfortunately, my mum, dad and brother weren't here because whenever my mum seems to come I don't do that well.

"Bless her, she is not banned from coming, but she avoids coming now."

The opener went on to make 126 from 105 deliveries, perfectly countering tricky early conditions - conditions in which Joe Root struggled uncharacteristically for 18 from 37 balls - and going on to share an increasingly aggressive stand of 150 in 117 balls with captain Harry Brook.

"To score a hundred for England is just the best feeling on earth," Banton said. "I don't think anything is going to beat it."

Brook made 77 and Jordan Cox, picked in the place of the injured Jos Buttler, added a 52-ball 76 to lift England to 355-7.

That always appeared a match-winning total on a surface offering bounce for the pace bowlers and turn for the spinners.

Sri Lanka crumbled to 132 all out in 29.1 overs, giving England a 223-run win and their biggest ODI victory against the tourists.

It meant England signed off their summer, one that included off-field issues, the end of Bazball, Ben Stokes' retirement and Root's surprise return as Test skipper, with a fifth successive series win amid the madness across formats.

Banton blasts England to series win

England thrash Sri Lanka by 223 runs to win ODI series - reaction, analysis & clips

Banton's success is heartwarming. When, fresh out of Second XI cricket, he made his debut as a 20-year-old in 2019 he was seen as England's next big thing.

He was in the same England Under-19 team as Brook but, rather than the Yorkshireman who is now captain, it was the Somerset product who was given the opportunity when Eoin Morgan's World Cup-winning side needed a fresh face on its journey forward.

Tougher times followed, resulting in almost five years out of the 50-over side and only occasional T20 appearances.

During that time Kevin Pietersen, now an England mentor, said Banton "has all the talent but, at the moment, he is wasting it".

It was comparisons to Pietersen which Banton struggled with. Last week, Banton said remains "in awe" of the iconic England batter.

With thrilling reverse sweeps here, he showed the invention that drew those comparisons. He was also vicious on the pull, hit classically through the covers and, when Ben Duckett was bowled in the second over and Root faced 13 dot balls in a row, did not panic.

When he walked off he turned and raised his bat amid a standing ovation from The Oval crowd – as Pietersen famously did 21 years ago.

Banton only has the opportunity as opener here because of Jacob Bethell's injury.

He may find himself out of the XI when England begin a tri-series in Pakistan - a series that also involves Sri Lanka - on 20 October.

The tourists, impressive in setting up this decider on Thursday, were poor here. They had already dropped Root before he was dismissed and wicketkeeper and captain Kusal Mendis spilled a thick edge when Brook had seven.

Afterwards the England captain started slowly but he kicked it into life from a position of 108-2 after 25 overs.

Also encouraging was the performance of Cox, whose knock also built on a slow start and followed an impressive run in the Test side against Pakistan.

Sonny Baker, recalled for his second ODI in place of Josh Tongue, nicked off Pathum Nissanka with a quick, swinging and rising delivery two balls into the second over, after which Sri Lanka did not recover. Left-arm spinner Liam Dawson also repaid the faith for his inclusion over Rehan Ahmed with figures of 3-26.

This summer has provided so many issues for England, including the end of Brendon McCullum's reign as Test coach.

Still his ODI side now has momentum - a third series win a row - as it builds towards next year's World Cup. Series in Pakistan, Australia and South Africa are to come this winter.

Back and loving it - Pietersen on his history, Brook & helping win the Ashes

title: Chelsea restore resilience - are they title contenders again?
description: Doubt crept in at Chelsea last season when they lost their Women's Super League crown - but early signs in this campaign suggest they have regained their spark for another challenge.
fullText:
Doubt crept in at Chelsea last season when they lost their Women's Super League crown - but early signs in this campaign suggest they have regained their spark.

A crucial 1-0 victory over rivals Arsenal on Sunday meant they extended their WSL unbeaten run to 12 games and sit just two points off leaders Manchester City.

They showed a different side - one that was willing to dig deep, control the game without the ball and defend with composure while Arsenal put pressure on.

It may have been the missing ingredient as Chelsea look revitalised and refreshed.

Could they win the WSL title this year? It would be foolish to say they can't.

Find interviews and extra content on the BBC Women's Football Weekly feed

Sonia Bompastor led Chelsea to an unbeaten domestic treble in her first season in charge, but it did not go to plan in 2025-26 as their six-year stranglehold on the WSL ended.

City overtook them at the top and many believed Arsenal would be the main challengers this season after a strong summer's recruitment.

Perhaps written off, Chelsea started the season tamely, drawing 1-1 with Aston Villa at Stamford Bridge despite a dominant performance.

The same issues were rife as they lacked ruthlessness in front of goal and a mistake at the back gifted Villa an opportunity.

But since then, Chelsea have turned dominant performances into results, winning three matches in a row, capping it off with a well-rounded display against Arsenal, who are seven points behind City in seventh spot.

Bompastor said her side were prepared to "mentally fight" and able to "adjust" to Arsenal's pressure in a way perhaps they didn't last season.

It was a defensive masterclass and they delivered Bompastor's gameplan perfectly, capping off victory with a third successive clean sheet - a run of 315 minutes without conceding a goal.

"In this league, you have so many different opponents and you have to be able to adjust and do something different," said the Blues boss.

"I've been talking a lot about that, to be strong and to be together, I always want to see a group of players who are together in those high and low moments.

"We came into this game well prepared. We knew we would have moments in the game where we were not in control. We prepared for those moments.

"We knew exactly where we wanted them to take the ball and where to leave some spaces. We were really strong mentally and physically."

It is a result that could be the catalyst Chelsea needed to push on and put pressure on Manchester City, who face Arsenal next in the WSL (Sunday, 16:30 BST).

Chelsea's match-winner Alyssa Thompson said their victory over the Gunners was "amazing for team morale".

Even Bompastor admitted Chelsea are "a different team from last season" and there are tangible examples of their improvements.

England midfielder Keira Walsh was a standout performer against Arsenal and it was her strike which was parried into the path of Thompson for the only goal.

Her new parternship with 20-year-old Lexi Potter is flourishing and has allowed Walsh to get further up the pitch and play with more freedom.

Bompastor said the 29-year-old was "a boss on the pitch" when she reaches those levels and it helps the team have "better foundations".

Goalscorer Thompson has consistently delivered up front, while the arrival of summer signing Melvine Malard from Manchester United has given them an outlet.

The French striker missed their opening two matches with a minor injury but scored on her debut against Birmingham City and caused havoc against Arsenal.

"She's massive for us. She puts in work off the ball and sets off the press," said team-mate Walsh.

"Her awareness of people around her and her ability... She's an incredible striker and she will be very good for us."

That press, led by Malard, has moved higher up and teams have struggled to break through, while full-back Ellie Carpenter continues to overlap dangerously.

Katie McCabe, who switched from Arsenal to Chelsea this summer, has brought leadership and bite - an aggression that was lacking at times last season.

Most of all, the Blues look like a team who believe they should be champions and are willing to work for it.

It was in contrast to toothless Arsenal, who have one victory in their first four WSL games and scored just twice.

"We've got both sides to our game and we showed that tonight in spells. Everyone was fighting for each other. Every first and second ball was ours," added Walsh.

title: Ex-CIA officer's novel alleges grave dysfunction in deep-cover operations
description:
A new, previously suppressed book by a former CIA officer paints a satirical and slashing portrait of the agency’s deep-cover spying program as riven by systematic dysfunction.
The book, “The Pickle Factory,” written by an ex-CIA nonofficial cover officer, under the pen name Sam R. Oyken, is billed as a work of fiction. Though often fantastical, it contains thinly veiled true-life details about the inner workings of the agency’s spying operations, according to former CIA officials.
Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post.
fullText:
A new, previously suppressed book by a former CIA officer paints a satirical and slashing portrait of the agency's deep-cover spying program as riven by systematic dysfunction.

The book, "The Pickle Factory," written by an ex-CIA nonofficial cover officer, under the pen name Sam R. Oyken, is billed as a work of fiction. Though often fantastical, it contains thinly veiled true-life details about the inner workings of the agency's spying operations, according to former CIA officials.

Most CIA officers work under what's known as "official cover" and generally masquerade as U.S. diplomats abroad. NOCs, who often pose as businessmen or consultants, have no overt connections to the U.S. government and therefore operate without diplomatic immunity.

Because of the potential dangers of their missions and the clandestine participation of American companies who provide cover to these officers, NOCs' operations are closely guarded inside the CIA.

"The Pickle Factory," published in late July, is the culmination of what the author characterized as a multiyear battle against agency censors, who first rejected publication of the manuscript in 2014. The Washington Post is referring to him by his pen name, as the former NOC remains undercover.

Former CIA employees are required to submit all work potentially relevant to their agency careers to the CIA's Prepublication Classification Review Board for potential redaction, to expunge it of allegedly classified information.

"They insisted for years after I submitted the manuscript of my novel that I couldn't publish a single word, a straight-up First Amendment violation," said Oyken in an interview.

Then-CIA Executive Director Meroe Park reversed the blanket ban in 2017, but the agency then "tried to redact more than half of the book, which I fought, redaction by redaction, until they folded," he said.

Park did not return a request for comment. A spokesperson for the CIA declined to comment.

The saga surrounding the book first trickled into public view in 2015, when Oyken - then using the alias Mack Charles in court documents - lodged a $25 million complaint against the CIA in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, alleging that agency officials conspired to fire the 13-year CIA veteran because they disapproved of his romantic relationship with another deep-cover officer to whom he was engaged and who was two decades younger.

Oyken was fired from the CIA in December 2010 and accused the agency of suppressing his book as part of a broader retaliation campaign, according to the 2015 lawsuit.

His suit against the agency was dismissed on procedural grounds in March 2016. The passage of time, and changes in agency leadership, appear to have attenuated concerns surrounding the book, and the CIA gave Oyken final approval to publish "The Pickle Factory" in early 2026.

Books by former NOCs have often met fierce resistance inside the CIA.

The 2019 publication of "Life Undercover," a memoir by former deep-cover officer Amaryllis Fox Kennedy, became embroiled in controversy when reports emerged that she did not receive final CIA approval to publish her book. Fox Kennedy - who served until recently as a senior official within the Office of the Director of National Intelligence and the Office of Management and Budget inside the Trump administration - did not appear to face sanction by the agency.

The CIA did sue another ex-NOC, writing under the pen name Ishmael Jones, for publishing a critical 2008 nonfiction account of his own experience inside the deep-cover program. Jones's book, "The Human Factor," had not been reviewed by agency censors. In 2012, a federal judge ordered Jones to forfeit any profit from future sales of the book.

"The Pickle Factory" dredges up what many CIA alumni consider an unhappy chapter in the history of the agency's deep-cover program.

In addition to skewering a number of former senior agency officials who oversaw the NOC cadre - whose biographies (and, at times, names) are only lightly fictionalized - the book recounts the agency's post-9/11 push to procure, and perhaps surreptitiously redirect for other purposes, billions of dollars in funding earmarked by Congress for a vastly expanded NOC program.

The post-9/11 NOC expansion was a real-life "debacle," said a former deep-cover colleague of Oyken's, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to candidly address sensitive intelligence operations, "where results were secondary, receipts were primary, and spending was king."

Much of Oyken's work with the agency remains shrouded in secrecy. His career bridged two eras at CIA, according to the same former colleague: the bespoke, targeted deep-cover program extant at CIA before Sept. 11, 2001, and the engorged NOC program that followed it, with younger, poorly trained NOCs being rushed into the field.

One part of this initiative involved deploying groups of these new NOCs to roughly a dozen secret "platforms" abroad; by 2008, almost all these efforts had folded in failure.

Oyken joined the CIA in 1996 as a French-speaking graduate of Harvard Law School who worked for the white-shoe law firm Covington & Burling before joining the agency, according to a declassified tranche of documents reviewed by The Post.

In 1999, he was selected for a 20-year deep-cover assignment abroad, an unusually long posting for NOC officers. The documents, some of which were redacted, point to a posting somewhere in Europe.

That assignment was cut short for reasons unclear in the declassified tranche reviewed by The Post. The mission ended because of a counterintelligence issue unrelated to Oyken's performance, according to another former CIA official who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe clandestine operations. Oyken was subsequently assigned to be an instructor to CIA trainees, according to the documents.

He was then selected for a managerial role inside the NOC program, according to court documents as well as the declassified tranche reviewed by The Post. Oyken is identified in the declassified papers as a "QRN," which former CIA colleagues say refers to "Quick Reaction NOC," an elite group of deep-cover officers who often travel on non-U.S. passports to undertake highly sensitive intelligence-gathering or eavesdropping-related missions abroad.

The court documents suggest that, after his stint as a trainer, Oyken served as QRN chief, stating that he "exercised supervisory authority over more than 80 subordinates, including other NOC Operations Officers in his Group."

Oyken's dismissal from the CIA was a contentious and bitter affair, per both sets of documents. His overseers accused him of financial improprieties, inappropriate romantic relationships with subordinates, absenteeism in his managerial duties and bullying of underlings. Agency officials also lamented his lack of recruitments, according to the declassified tranche.

His was "a chronic case of long-term behavior that has completely eroded the confidence management has in this officer," said one declassified agency memorandum reviewed by The Post.

Oyken strenuously contested the allegations. "They came at me like a pack of wild dogs," he said in an interview.

The declassified documents reveal an aggressive investigation into Oyken, including his finances. In one partially redacted 2009 email, an incoming NOC program chief decries the "loose approach" to deep-cover deployments, vowing that Oyken "will be coming home the first day I'm in the chair." He was "the kind of china I'm looking forward to breaking" upon taking over the program, writes the soon-to-be NOC boss.

Oyken characterizes the deep-cover program as hidebound and in acute need of reform. "There's a certain kind of CIA manager who prefers that NOCs be full-time accountants rather than spies out taking risks," he said. "Meanwhile they themselves squander billions of dollars and turn a blind eye while their cronies make off with stacks of gold bars."

In May 2026, David J. Rush, a senior CIA official working on ultrasecret intelligence-gathering programs, was arrested on charges of stealing public funds, including the alleged theft of $40 million worth of gold bars from the agency.

Though formally a work of fiction, "The Pickle Factory" clearly puts the real-world CIA in its crosshairs. "It's almost impossible for outsiders to grasp how mediocre the agency has become," Oyken said. "Only a novel-length treatment could do the topic justice."

title: Christa Pike could be the 1st woman executed in Tennessee in 200 years
description: Christa Pike's lawyers have filed a clemency petition seeking to commute her sentence ahead of the 30 September execution date  [Tennesse Department of...
fullText:
Ashlee Sellars last heard from her friend Christa Pike earlier this week, when Pike texted her from her cell on death row as she prepares to be killed by lethal injection by the US state of Tennessee.

Pike told Sellars she did not want any of her loved ones to be present on Wednesday when she is executed.

"She doesn't want us to experience that," Sellars says.

Sellars finds it hard to reconcile this woman, whom she has only known to be kind and protective, with the person who committed a heinous crime 31 years ago.

Pike, now 50, was 18 when she and her boyfriend at the time, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and murdered Colleen Slemmer, a 19-year-old they met at a job training camp for troubled teens.

The murder created a media frenzy in Knoxville, Tennessee in 1995, when Colleen was found with a pentagram - a symbol of Satanic ritual - carved into her chest.

Pike had accused Colleen of insulting her and trying to steal her boyfriend. Two other residents at the camp later testified that Pike had bragged about the murder before and after, and showed them a piece of Colleen's skull.

A year later she was sentenced to death, while Shipp - who was 17 at the time - was given a life sentence with the possibility of parole.

Now, after years of failed appeals, Pike's execution has been set. If it goes ahead, she will be the first woman put to death in Tennessee in more than 200 years. Only 18 women have been executed in the US since the 1970s, compared to 1,663 men.

Colleen's mother has said she wants Pike's execution to happen so that her daughter "finally can be resting".

But Pike's lawyers, who filed a 226-page clemency petition, are still hoping for a last-minute reprieve, while UN human rights experts have also called for the execution to be stopped.

Pike has a documented history of childhood sexual abuse, abandonment and neglect. Her lawyers believe that if she was found guilty of the same crime today as a teenager she would not receive a death sentence.

In the years since her sentencing, her defence team have uncovered details about her childhood that they say the jury never had the chance to consider.

"It is mind-boggling that they did not present any of her history of abuse and rape, even though they knew about it," says Sandra Babcock, an expert in gender and the death penalty at Cornell Law School, who has worked on Pike's defence.

"Her case is so uniquely compelling, not just because of her really incomprehensible history of sexual violence but the combination of that with her youth and her mental illness."

In 1995, forensic psychologist Dr Diana McCoy was hired by Pike's defence team and found she was severely neglected by both of her parents.

McCoy's report found Pike was physically and sexually abused by several of her mother's husbands and boyfriends, and raped several times, once when she was 11 and again aged 17. Later, it was discovered that she was repeatedly raped as a toddler by her grandmother's boyfriend. McCoy said Pike's mother didn't believe her that these rapes happened.

But Pike's trial lawyer did not put McCoy on the stand or call many of the witnesses she recommended. These details emerged over a decade later in a court hearing reviewing her case, when a new team of lawyers claimed ineffective assistance of counsel, a claim that was denied by the judge.

In 2021, Pike was diagnosed with bipolar disorder in prison and has been medicated since.

Later, another forensic psychologist working for Pike's defence, Dr Bethany Brand, who assessed Pike in 2023, said her case was extremely rare because she was abused by so many people who should have protected her.

"Her childhood was replete with physical, sexual and emotional abuse. She was sexually violated by a number of men, starting before she was school age," she says.

Brand says Pike had untreated manic episodes due to bipolar disorder and untreated PTSD.

"Both of those things together absolutely influenced how threatened she felt by the girl she ended up killing and her lack of emotional control in that situation."

Babcock adds: "If they let her be executed, then what it tells us is that the death penalty in this country is just a joke. It's not for the worst of the worst. It is for the people who receive the worst legal representation and who are the most damaged and vulnerable."

Last year, Tennessee's Supreme Court ruled Pike had not shown circumstances that would justify commuting her sentence. Her appeals process had been exhausted and a date was set for her execution.

A federal appeals court had earlier ruled that the jury had already heard about her difficult childhood during testimony from her mother, father and aunt during her trial. And that new evidence of bipolar disorder, PTSD and brain damage "mostly repeated" what the jury had heard and would not have changed the verdict.

The row has some parallels with the high-profile case of murderer Lisa Montgomery, whose lawyers also argued she was a mentally ill victim of abuse who deserved mercy.

Montgomery's legal challenges failed to commute her sentence and she was executed by lethal injection in Indiana in 2021.

Unless she is granted clemency by Tennessee Governor Bill Lee, Pike will be executed on 30 September. That decision is unlikely to come until the last moment and Lee has never before granted clemency in a death penalty case.

The Tennessee Supreme Court this week denied Pike's request to halt the execution. Her counsel say they have been discussing next steps.

On her execution day, Pike has requested an all-female team. She says being held down by a group of men will exacerbate her trauma. The state of Tennessee has said the goal is that female guards will transfer Pike to the prison where she will be executed but hasn't guaranteed it.

Colleen's mother May Martinez supports Christa's execution.

"She did the crime. I think she should pay for it," she said on Knoxville TV station WBIR in 2021, and told the BBC this week she still stands by those comments.

Pike should suffer before she dies, Martinez told WBIR. "I would feel better that she felt the same pain that Colleen did."

"My heart breaks every single day because I keep reliving it and reliving it, and I can't no more, and I want this to happen before I die," she added.

"There's not a day goes by that I don't think about Colleen or how she died and how rough it was. I just want Christa down so I can end it, relieve my daughter, so she finally can be resting."

The Justice Coalition, a victims' rights advocacy group, has raised money to help Martinez travel to Tennessee to watch the execution.

The group's executive director, Robert Bracewell, said this sentence was determined by a jury of Pike's peers and it was what Colleen's family want.

"We stand firm with the family that on the 30 September her execution ought to proceed."

Ashlee Sellars grapples with two seemingly conflicting beliefs: that Colleen's mother has a right to feel justice has been served and that everyone, including her friend Christa, deserves a chance at redemption.

"When I think about reconciling who you see on TV or the horrible tragedy that happened with Colleen, the only thing that makes sense to me is around mental health and trauma and the way that people process stuff in a moment when they don't have the things that they need," Sellars says.

"These horrible things happen in your youth and then those traumas moved through you, in our community, and you cause harm to somebody else."

Sellars met Pike in prison while serving a 25-year sentence for her involvement in a robbery-murder. They spoke to each other through the meal flaps in their doors on the high security unit. Now, Sellars works as an advocate for justice reform and victims of crime.

"People want to know that everyone's life matters, right? They want to know that Colleen's life mattered," she says.

"Christa in this moment, I think she is fighting much more for her life to matter than she is to actually live."

title: Air Force One does a flyover at country club as Trump visits first tee at Presidents Cup
description:
Donald Trump is the latest U.S. president to attend the festivities at the international biennial match-play competition, the Presidents Cup, doing so for a second time.
The competition features a 12-man American squad vs. a 12-man International team.
fullText:
Donald Trump is the latest U.S. president to attend the festivities at the international biennial match-play competition, the Presidents Cup, doing so for a second time.

The competition features a 12-man American squad vs. a 12-man International team.

Sunday morning, Air Force One made its approach in the Chicagoland area and did a flyover at Medinah Country Club.

After touching down, Trump's motorcade made its way to Medinah, host of the 16th Presidents Cup.

Trump spoke briefly with reporters after landing in Chicago, saying, “You'll be seeing the best players, the best golfers anywhere in the world. It's going to be great. I think for those of you that don't play, you'll get it," he said ahead of his arrival to Medinah.

Fans were alerted 12 hours prior to expect delays and enhanced security measures and additional restrictions.

Gates opened at 8 a.m. and fans quickly filled the first tee, though, in anticipation of an American comeback. The U.S. started the final day down 10½ to 7½.

Trump walked out to the trophy stand at the first tee at Medinah to loud cheers and some lesser scattered boos that were drowned out by "U-S-A!" chants. He was then introduced by the CEO of the PGA Tour, Brian Rolapp.

Golfweek reported Saturday that Trump had requested to speak at the first tee for 15 minutes before the start of play but that didn't occur. Instead, Trump made some brief remarks, joking he was not brave enough to subject the crowd to a speech, then jabbed at the "fake news media", whom he joked would report he received a poor reception, before posing for pictures.

A few fans chanted out "four more years" in the stands behind him before Trump smiled and waved to the crowd a few more times, then departed.

Trump then hung out on the first tee, shaking hands with each U.S. player ahead of their opening tee shots.

A month ago, Trump accepted the role of honorary chairman for Presidents Cup, a tradition he is continuing. Previous Presidents Cup honorary chairs:

Keep up with Golfweek all weekend for all the latest news from the 2026 Presidents Cup.

title: Trump reaffirms ICE arrest policy after confusing guidance alarms agents
description:
The Trump administration denied reports Saturday evening that Immigration and Customs Enforcement had temporarily instructed agents to limit arrests to illegal immigrants with criminal records.
The clarification comes as immigration enforcement remains a central pillar of President Donald Trump’s agenda. The administration has promised an aggressive crackdown on illegal immigration and expanded deportations, and officials said that effort has not been scaled back.
Trump Administration's Immigration Push Fuels Ice's Biggest Arrest Month In Agency History
President Donald Trump has made immigration enforcement a central pillar of his administration, promising a sweeping crackdown on illegal immigration and expanded deportations.
Fox News correspondent Bill Melugin, who spoke with Trump and nine ICE and Department of Homeland Security sources, reported that verbal guidance instructing field offices to prioritize the "worst first" was distributed nationwide earlier this week.
fullText:
The Trump administration denied reports Saturday evening that Immigration and Customs Enforcement had temporarily instructed agents to limit arrests to illegal immigrants with criminal records.

The clarification comes as immigration enforcement remains a central pillar of President Donald Trump’s agenda. The administration has promised an aggressive crackdown on illegal immigration and expanded deportations, and officials said that effort has not been scaled back.

TRUMP ADMINISTRATION'S IMMIGRATION PUSH FUELS ICE'S BIGGEST ARREST MONTH IN AGENCY HISTORY

Fox News correspondent Bill Melugin, who spoke with Trump and nine ICE and Department of Homeland Security sources, reported that verbal guidance instructing field offices to prioritize the "worst first" was distributed nationwide earlier this week.

The guidance alarmed some ICE agents, who described it as shocking and frustrating, Melugin wrote on X.

Sources later said the confusion stemmed from internal conversations about prioritizing the most serious offenders and that the directive was the result of a "miscommunication," rather than a formal change in policy.

"There is no change in immigration enforcement policy," Melugin wrote on X.

New guidance was sent to ICE field offices Saturday evening to reaffirm that the administration’s enforcement policy had not changed, according to the sources.

DHS BOSS REVEALS OVAL OFFICE PLAN TO 'WITHHOLD FUNDING' FROM SANCTUARY CITIES AFTER AGGRESSIVE NEW YORK BUST

Trump told Fox News that ICE can still arrest and deport anyone who is in the country illegally.

ICE agents will also continue arresting illegal immigrants without additional criminal histories, including "collaterals," or individuals encountered during an operation targeting someone else.

The sources said the administration’s broader immigration enforcement agenda remains in place.

title: Waltz says Iran wanted sanctions relief first. Tehran says that's not the full story.
description:
Mike Waltz, U.S. ambassador to the United Nations, said Sunday that President Donald Trump rejected Iran's latest proposal because Tehran wanted sanctions relief and access to "billions in frozen assets" before negotiating an end to its nuclear program.
"They were asking for everything up front, with a promise that they would then talk," Waltz said on CNN's "State of the Union" when asked what Trump objected to.
In a separate interview on NBC's "Meet the Press," Waltz called the proposal "a pretty cynical attempt to put something on the table that they knew was unacceptable.
fullText:
Mike Waltz, U.S. ambassador to the United Nations, said Sunday that President Donald Trump rejected Iran's latest proposal because Tehran wanted sanctions relief and access to "billions in frozen assets" before negotiating an end to its nuclear program.

"They were asking for everything up front, with a promise that they would then talk," Waltz said on CNN's "State of the Union" when asked what Trump objected to.

In a separate interview on NBC's "Meet the Press," Waltz called the proposal "a pretty cynical attempt to put something on the table that they knew was unacceptable." He said the U.S. would ultimately need to reach "some type of agreement" with Iran, but Trump would keep all options on the table.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, in an interview later on the same NBC program, pushed back on Waltz's account and told host Kristen Welker that Iran was prepared to open the strait if the U.S. met its conditions, including releasing frozen assets and allowing Iranian oil sales.

"I am surprised that the ambassador is talking about a seven-day plan, as he has not read it," Araghchi said. "Maybe he has not been given a copy."

On Saturday, Trump rejected an Iranian proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and resume nuclear talks in exchange for the U.S. lifting its naval blockade of Iranian ports, waiving sanctions on Iranian oil sales and committing to a seven-day ceasefire that would include Lebanon.

In an interview with CBS's "Face the Nation" recorded Friday and aired Sunday, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian described the proposal as a staged approach based on an earlier U.S.-Iran agreement.

"Ultimately, the requests that were included in that memorandum and MOU have now been broken down into stages so that we can proceed according to those stages," Pezeshkian said. "These are things that both sides need to open up first, then we can sit down at the negotiating table and discuss other issues at hand."

"They wanna make a deal where they open the Strait immediately because they're losing so badly," Trump told reporters. "We're winning tremendously. We have total control of the Hormuz Strait."

The Wall Street Journal reported Friday, citing U.S. officials, that Trump has told aides he expected to resume bombing Iran after the November midterms.

Asked about the report, Waltz said, "I don't think that the president has said that himself; that's some reporting by a newspaper."

"What the president has said and said here at his U.N. speech was that the Iranians are miscalculating that he's taking into account politics here," Waltz added.

On "Meet the Press," Waltz also declined to confirm the reported timetable, saying Trump would "leave all options on the table."

Araghchi, asked about the same report, said Iran was "fully prepared for the war to be resumed" but remained open to diplomacy. "It is up to President Trump to choose," he said.

This comes as the war in Iran and rising gas prices put pressure on Republicans ahead of the November midterms.

title: Republicans pour money into dozens of House races previously considered 'safe'
description:
NEW YORK, Sept 27 (Reuters) - Republicans are pouring money into more than three dozen US House races previously considered “safe” after internal polling showed they could be vulnerable in the November 3 election, according to three Republican operatives familiar with the party’s thinking. 
   The shift is already starting to show in advertising reservations and campaign finance filings. Since September 1, major Republican groups and megadonors have begun ‌spending in at least 39 congressional races where they haven’t previously deployed money this cycle, a Reuters review of spending by some of the largest Republican political groups shows. 
   Many of the candidates receiving new support ‌sit in Republican strongholds and are still running ahead of Democratic opponents in public polls, these people said, indicating rising worry among party leaders over whether voters will use the November 3 election to air dissatisfaction over US President Donald Trump’s policies. 
   House Republican leaders recently warned dozens of ​campaigns that the party's internal data shows that they cannot assume they will win, even if they are currently ahead in public polls and represent districts Trump won by double digits, two of the people said.
fullText:
NEW YORK, Sept 27 (Reuters) - Republicans are pouring money into more than three dozen US House races previously considered "safe" after internal polling showed they could be vulnerable in the November 3 election, according to three Republican operatives familiar with the party's thinking.

The shift is already starting to show in advertising reservations and campaign finance filings. Since September 1, major Republican groups and megadonors have begun ‌spending in at least 39 congressional races where they haven't previously deployed money this cycle, a Reuters review of spending by some of the largest Republican political groups shows.

Many of the candidates receiving new support ‌sit in Republican strongholds and are still running ahead of Democratic opponents in public polls, these people said, indicating rising worry among party leaders over whether voters will use the November 3 election to air dissatisfaction over US President Donald Trump's policies.

House Republican leaders recently warned dozens of ​campaigns that the party's internal data shows that they cannot assume they will win, even if they are currently ahead in public polls and represent districts Trump won by double digits, two of the people said.

"Republicans are playing defense in some of the strongholds that they're used to not having to worry about," said Republican strategist Ron Bonjean, a partner at bipartisan public affairs firm Rokk Solutions.

Republicans currently hold a narrow 218-214 majority in the House, with one independent caucusing with Republicans and two vacancies. Democrats would need to net at least four seats in the midterms to take control of the chamber next year.

Two Republican operatives working with party leaders said they're using their larger spending power to stifle Democrats before they ‌have a chance to attack. They said the party was taking out "insurance policies" ⁠to ensure Republican-held districts remain in the party's hands.

"Republicans are deploying our massive war chest to drive voters to the polls and supercharge our candidates," said Natalie Baldassarre, national press secretary for the Republican National Committee. "We're not taking anything for granted, because, unlike Democrats, Republicans aren't throwing in the towel on races we can win."

Republican Representative Bryan Steil is one telling ⁠example. His Wisconsin district voted for Trump by about 4.5 percentage points in 2024 and is rated "lean Republican" by Cook Political Report. Still, conservative super PACs dumped $1.5 million on his race this month, their first investment of this election cycle. A representative for Steil declined to comment.

In North Carolina's 3rd Congressional District east of Raleigh, Representative Gregory Murphy this month received $131,107 from a conservative PAC a week ago – the first outside spending on his behalf in the midterms. Democrats have spent over $326,000 trying to oust him since ​July. ​Trump won the district by 14 percentage points and Cook rates it "solid Republican." Murphy's office didn't return a request for comment.

The emergency ​deployments reflect a harsh reality: economic strain is battering traditionally Republican strongholds. Rising gas prices, ‌energy costs and fertilizer expenses are hitting voters in the agricultural heartland particularly hard.

One Republican House campaign aide said the environment for candidates in Iowa, Kansas and other Midwest states was "dire" as diesel prices soar.

"We're in this crucial period in the last 30 days where candidates have to really make a case, given how tough the headwinds are," said Kevin Madden, who advised former Republican presidential candidate Mitt Romney and is now senior partner at corporate advisory firm Penta Group. Campaigns are running as if they are behind in the polls "even in red districts or traditionally safe" ones, Madden said.

More than $1.56 billion, overall, has been spent by independent committees on federal elections so far, with roughly $496 million deployed just since Labor Day, according to a Reuters analysis of super PAC spending. That figure doesn't include all spending by dark money nonprofits that do not disclose their donors.

Republicans have reserved at least $888 million in advertising over the coming weeks, compared ‌to at least $666 million for Democrats, according to AdImpact, which tracks political advertising. No Going Back PAC, which is fully funded by ​Trump's super PAC MAGA Inc., is leading the surge, Federal Election Commission records show.

"That's the advantage of having a shit ton of money," ​said one Republican operative working on Trump's midterm strategy. "We're not going to let Democrats take free shots on ​goal."

Over the last three weeks through Frday, Republican-leaning super PACs have outspent Democrats by almost 2-to-1, showering races with roughly $309.7 million since Labor Day compared with $174.2 million going to help Democratic ‌candidates, the FEC data shows.

"Republicans have air superiority. House Democrats are scrambling to catch ​up with the very limited resources they have," said Mike ​Marinella, national press secretary for the National Republican Congressional Committee, which works to elect Republicans to the House.

Democrats acknowledge their funding disadvantage but say the Republican push to spend money on districts that Trump won easily reflects the trouble the party faces in the midterms.

"Republicans are running scared, know they've lost the American people, and are trying one last hail mary to spend their way out of certain defeat," said Viet ​Shelton, spokesman for the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee.

In one district in south Texas that Trump won ‌by 18 percentage points in 2024, Republican groups have pumped about $2 million into text messages, direct mail and digital ads since September 5 to help incumbent Representative Monica De La Cruz keep her seat. Cook Political ​Report moved her seat from "lean Republican" to "tossup" on Friday.

De La Cruz is grateful for her supporters helping defeat her rival, her campaign manager said, when asked about the money spent by her ​Republican backers.

title: Susan Collins is back on the ballot for the first time since Roe was overturned
description:
— For years, Planned Parenthood’s endorsement of Susan Collins was enough to persuade Erin Evans to vote for Maine's longtime U.S. senator, believing that the moderate Republican would protect abortion access.
Evans is now “just furious with myself” for those votes. The 56-year-old from Portland described Collins’ critical vote to confirm Brett Kavanaugh to the U.
fullText:
GORHAM, Maine (AP) — For years, Planned Parenthood's endorsement of Susan Collins was enough to persuade Erin Evans to vote for Maine's longtime U.S. senator, believing that the moderate Republican would protect abortion access.

Evans is now "just furious with myself" for those votes. The 56-year-old from Portland described Collins' critical vote to confirm Brett Kavanaugh to the U.S. Supreme Court, where President Donald Trump's nominee eventually helped overturn the constitutional right to abortion, as a betrayal.

"I was a really uninformed voter," Evans said. "I thought any woman from Maine was probably in line with me."

The Nov. 3 election will be the first time Collins is on the ballot since the Supreme Court's 2022 ruling that overturned Roe v. Wade, resulting in abortion being banned in much of the United States. This time, Evans says she is backing Democrat Troy Jackson, a former state lawmaker and logger trying to deny Collins a sixth term.

Jackson and Democrats are hoping that voters like Evans will help flip a seat in a state the party has made a priority in the quest to retake the Senate.

Both Collins and Jackson have made an effort to appeal to women, who make up the majority of Maine's population and have had a slightly higher rate of voting than men, according to a recent report by democracy advocacy groups. In campaign ads from both candidates, women are featured prominently.

Democrats' ads have focused heavily on Collins' vote in support of Kavanaugh and describe her as caving to Trump. The Democratic-aligned advocacy group Affordable Maine has spent nearly $10 million on ads stressing the senator's backing of other Trump-appointed judges who oppose abortion. An additional $32 million has been spent by Win Senate, a political action committee focused on Collins. Planned Parenthood Votes has so far spent at least $500,000 to run ads that include a female voter who regrets voting for Collins because of her Kavanaugh vote.

Yet Jackson is facing a steep challenge.

Collins has a 30-year record of winning elections even as Maine voters have spurned Republican presidential nominees, including Trump, since 1988.

And the issue trails others in terms of importance to voters. A New York Times/Siena poll conducted in September found that when asked in their own words what one issue will be most important in deciding their vote for Congress in November, almost no likely Maine voters mentioned abortion.

Collins has long called herself a "pro-choice" Republican and a supporter of a woman's right to an abortion. She was one of the few Republicans endorsed by Planned Parenthood earlier in her political career. In 2022, she co-sponsored legislation to put federal protections for abortion into law.

The position has put her at odds with her party but was in line with Maine voters.

In 2020, the last time Collins sought reelection, the vast majority of Maine voters in the Senate race, 76%, said the Supreme Court should not overturn Roe v. Wade, according to AP VoteCast, an extensive survey of the electorate. That included most Collins voters. Some 35% of voters who supported Collins in her successful reelection bid said they wanted Roe to be overturned.

Collins' 2018 vote in support of Kavanaugh was crucial to his confirmation. At the time, Collins waited months before announcing her decision in a 45-minute floor speech. The final vote was 50-48.

Kavanaugh later joined the 6-3 conservative majority in stripping away constitutional rights to abortion.

Collins criticized the high court's decision in 2022, but she has never publicly wavered in her decision to confirm Kavanaugh. She told reporters in June that "I do not regret that vote." Collins had said before the 2018 vote that Kavanaugh, in a two-hour meeting with her, said he viewed Roe as settled law.

But her confirmation vote is what stands out in the minds of voters like Bente Lundh, 67, of Falmouth.

"She's positioned herself as this moderate voter, but she's really chopped that down with her vote for Kavanaugh," Lundh said.

For others, Collins' long-standing record as a moderate continues to draw their support even if they are disappointed with the eventual overturning of Roe.

"I think I've tried to not have my allegiance to party make me blind to what may be a better path from time to time," said Mary Ann Lynch, a Democrat supporting Collins. "Neither party, in my view, has a monopoly on the truth and how best to do things. So I think it's really important to have people who will reach across the aisle."

Lynch added that Collins may have voted to confirm Kavanaugh, but she also voted to confirm Supreme Court Justices Sonia Sotomayor and Elena Kagan, who dissented in the abortion ruling. They were nominated by Democratic President Barack Obama.

Since launching his campaign in July, Jackson has announced a "Women for Troy" coalition made up of women from all 16 Maine counties and he has secured endorsements from abortion rights groups Planned Parenthood and Reproductive Freedom for All.

Jackson was serving as a top state senator when the landmark 1973 decision was upended in 2022. He says he worked to pass "some of the strongest protections for abortion access in the country."

Yet Jackson has had his own hurdles.

The Democrat became a last-minute Senate nominee after Graham Platner dropped out this summer following criticism of his past relationships with women and a sexual assault allegation, which Platner denies. Jackson is now scrambling to win over voters who may be wary of his connection to Platner. The two campaigned together as Jackson initially sought the Democratic gubernatorial nomination but lost.

Jackson also has had to explain the evolution of his support on abortion rights and same-sex marriage, both of which he opposed years ago. Jackson now says he was wrong about his past beliefs and changed his mind after talking to women. Jackson's campaign spokesperson Maggie Amjad said Jackson now holds a "100% rating from Maine's Planned Parenthood."

Blake Kernen, a spokesperson for Collins, described the senator as the only "reliably pro-choice" candidate in the race.

While Jackson is reminding voters of Collins' role in the abortion rights fight, he is doing so in a state that was not highly affected by the decision compared with Republican-controlled regions where many abortion clinics have shuttered, said Mark Brewer, a political science professor at the University of Maine.

"If you were in a state where all of the abortion clinics had closed, then that might be a bigger issue," Brewer said. "That has not been the case here."

The state's Democratic-controlled Legislature in 2023 approved a law that allows abortions at any time if deemed medically necessary by a doctor, and Democratic Gov. Janet Mills has enacted legislation protecting providers of abortion and gender-affirming care from legal action brought by other states.

A CNN/SSRS survey of likely Maine voters conducted in late August and early September found that most voters are still unhappy about the decision to overturn Roe, but that anger over the loss of abortion rights could be overshadowed by broader concerns about the economy.

Kruesi reported from Providence, R.I. Associated Press polling editor Amelia Thomson DeVeaux in Washington contributed to this report.

title: Sea level rise is reshaping a California beach town and threatening a key rail line
description:
SAN CLEMENTE, Calif. (AP) — For years, residents of this Southern California beach town could walk a mile along a stretch of cream-colored sand and dip their toes in the waves lapping ashore.
That trip has been cut short.
Coastal erosion has been eating away at the beach in San Clemente, known for nearly a century as a “Spanish village by the sea.” The rising sea and crashing waves have pushed the shoreline landward, splitting the city's picturesque North Beach.
fullText:
SAN CLEMENTE, Calif. (AP) — For years, residents of this Southern California beach town could walk a mile along a stretch of cream-colored sand and dip their toes in the waves lapping ashore.

Coastal erosion has been eating away at the beach in San Clemente, known for nearly a century as a "Spanish village by the sea." The rising sea and crashing waves have pushed the shoreline landward, splitting the city's picturesque North Beach. Crumbling seaside bluffs have damaged oceanfront homes and forced the repeated closure of a passenger rail line considered the second busiest in the country.

It's one of many California coastal communities grappling with the effects of sea level rise. Nearly a decade ago, scientists forecast that more than half of Southern California's beaches could significantly erode by 2100, radically altering how people live and recreate along the state's famed coast.

"The constant pressure is sea level rise," said Sean Vitousek, research oceanographer with the U.S. Geological Survey. "It is going to keep rising, and rising, and the beaches will retreat landward."

After years of erosion, California is bracing for flooding and landslides ahead of this year's expected super El Niño, a temporary warming in parts of the equatorial Pacific known to warp weather worldwide. Already this year, the town of Pacifica south of San Francisco shuttered its cracked concrete pier, and seawater flooded homes in Long Beach near Los Angeles during a hurricane-driven storm surge. A recent study showed that El Niño events are getting stronger because of human-caused climate change.

In San Clemente, a town of 62,000 people, urban development has slowed the flow of sediment that once nourished the city's beaches, and warmer ocean waters have pushed waves higher and further ashore. It's become so challenging that residents of the largely Republican city are considering taxing themselves to raise money for beach restoration. A measure to add a 1% sales tax to fund wildfire protection and sand replenishment in San Clemente is on the November ballot.

Over the past five years, the rail line that has operated along the coast for more than a century has faced repeated closures due to encroaching surf on one side and fragile bluffs on the other. The 7-mile (11-kilometer) segment is part of a 351-mile (565-kilometer) passenger rail corridor that links San Diego with Los Angeles County's huge port complex and San Luis Obispo. It's also used by freight and the military.

Transportation officials have shored up the tracks to ensure passenger safety by laying down rock. But as waves slam against the rocks, they sweep more sand offshore and speed up erosion that will eventually threaten the rail line again.

Locals say the erosion is dramatically altering their community.

"We've lost our walkable beach," said Cameron Cosgrove, a San Clemente resident who wrote the tax measure. "It used to be you could come to North Beach, walk the beach trail, or on the beach to the pier and actually all the way down to the south end of town. Can't do either anymore."

City and transit officials agree more sand is needed and note that coastal communities, including surf hub Huntington Beach, have nourished their beaches for years. Opponents of the measure want sand — but not the tax — and argue San Clemente should work with other communities on a regional approach.

"Fighting Mother Nature is very expensive," said City Councilman Zhen Wu, who opposes the measure.

City Manager Andy Hall said San Clemente faces a sand deficit of about 3 million cubic yards. Getting that much sand to the beach is no easy task, he said, adding that trucking it would require 300,000 trips.

Darrell Johnson, chief executive of the Orange County Transportation Authority, said a challenge has been getting state permits for more sand. He hopes California's recent emergency declaration ahead of El Niño will speed up the process. In the long run, Johnson said officials will study moving trains inland — an idea previously deemed too costly. A third option is to halt the line, he said.

"If we can't figure out how to shore up properly in a way that is long-term in nature, and we can't figure out how to relocate, I think that is a question that's going to have to be asked," Johnson said. "'What happens to passenger rail? What happens to freight?'"

Further south, transportation officials have been working to stabilize coastal bluffs to shore up the rail line in the community of Del Mar. The plan is to eventually move the tracks, but officials have not decided where.

Charlie Fox, a 56-year-old San Clemente resident and marine meteorologist, said sand provides a critical buffer between whatever structures — train tracks, homes, lifeguard headquarters — are built along the coast. The lifelong surfer said sand also helps waves roll gently onshore, creating a steady wave break for surfing.

On a recent morning, surfers bobbed in the water off North Beach, not far from the rocky structure shoring up the train tracks by the sea.

"When you see those rocks, that's them attempting to fight the ocean," Fox said. "That is a futile endeavor."

"The ocean wins," he added. "Ocean always eventually wins."

title: White House airs taxpayer-funded Trump ‘final battle’ ad ahead of midterms
description:
President Donald Trump appears in a television ad. - US Government
The White House has launched another taxpayer-funded television ad before the midterms, this time featuring imagery of President Donald Trump walking down a hall as audio plays of him saying “this is the final battle.”
“We will cast out the communists, Marxists, and fascists. We will throw off the sick political class that hates our country. We will rout the fake news media, and we will liberate America from these villains once and for all,” Trump says in the ad, echoing comments he made during a Veterans Day speech in 2023.
fullText:
The White House has launched another taxpayer-funded television ad before the midterms, this time featuring imagery of President Donald Trump walking down a hall as audio plays of him saying “this is the final battle.”

“We will cast out the communists, Marxists, and fascists. We will throw off the sick political class that hates our country. We will rout the fake news media, and we will liberate America from these villains once and for all,” Trump says in the ad, echoing comments he made during a Veterans Day speech in 2023.

The ad aired during at least two NFL games on Sunday, during Fox’s broadcasts of the Washington Commanders-Seattle Seahawks matchup as well as the Carolina Panthers-Cleveland Browns game.

The Trump administration has drawn widespread attention for its airing of ads featuring the president just over a month before the November midterms. The White House has compared the ads to previous administrations running public service announcements about Medicare, Obamacare and promoting Covid-19 vaccination, saying in a statement that its new commercials “are very clearly not campaign ads.”

The latest ad appears nearly identical to the majority of a video Trump posted on Truth Social in January 2024, during his third presidential campaign. The video on Truth Social has an additional six seconds that includes Trump’s campaign logo and a number to text, while “Paid for by the US Government” is seen across the screen at the end of the White House-funded ad.

This is the third government-funded ad to be captured in recent days by the media tracker AdImpact. An ad that began airing Wednesday featured rapidly edited pictures and video of Trump over audio of him denouncing communism and socialism, with text on the screen that touts his administration’s accomplishments, such as “reigniting American manufacturing.”

A second ad features video of Trump at Mount Rushmore as his voice is heard saying, “Never before has any nation celebrated so magnificent a triumph as this one.”

The White House declined to elaborate on how the first ad was being funded but defended it as part of “public service announcements” to promote national pride.

“The ad is educational and unapologetically patriotic,” a White House spokesperson said in a statement. “We should be proud of our country.”

That ad drew scrutiny from the government watchdog group Common Cause, which suggested it could violate rules against using taxpayer dollars for “propaganda.”

“I don’t think you have to be a legal scholar and wonder why the president has to use taxpayer funds to promote his image” this close to an election, Carol Evans, the vice president for policy at Common Cause, told CNN.
